title: USMLE Step 1
issuer: National Board of Medical Examiners / FSMB
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public USMLE Step 1 content outline. Not a capture of past test questions.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of progressive abdominal distention and slow growth. Examination shows a markedly enlarged liver, and laboratory testing during an overnight fast shows hypoglycemia, marked lactic acidosis, hypertriglyceridemia and hyperuricemia. A deficiency of which enzyme best explains this constellation?
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase in hepatocytes
Acid alpha-glucosidase in lysosomes
Glycogen debranching enzyme
Hepatic phosphorylase kinase
items.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate during both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so its absence causes fasting hypoglycemia with upstream accumulation that is shunted to lactate, triglycerides and uric acid. Cori disease from debranching enzyme deficiency causes milder fasting hypoglycemia without prominent lactic acidosis, and Pompe disease from acid maltase deficiency causes myopathy with cardiomegaly rather than this hepatic picture.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A purified enzyme is assayed at increasing substrate concentrations in the presence of a reversible inhibitor that binds a site distinct from the active site. Even at saturating substrate the reaction velocity never reaches the uninhibited maximum, while the substrate concentration that gives one-half maximal velocity is unchanged. Which inhibition pattern is demonstrated?
options: Noncompetitive inhibition with a reduced maximal velocity and an unchanged half-saturation constant
Competitive inhibition with an unchanged maximal velocity and an increased apparent half-saturation constant
Uncompetitive inhibition with parallel reductions in maximal velocity and half-saturation constant
Irreversible inactivation of catalytic residues by a suicide substrate
items.explanation: An inhibitor binding somewhere other than the active site removes functional enzyme molecules from the reaction, so maximal velocity falls while substrate affinity is unchanged in the pure noncompetitive case. Competitive inhibition can be overcome by enough substrate so maximal velocity is preserved, uncompetitive inhibition lowers both maximal velocity and the apparent half-saturation constant, and irreversible inactivation is not reversed by removing the inhibitor.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 6-year-old child develops marked freckling of sun-exposed skin and has already undergone excision of two squamous cell carcinomas of the nose. Fibroblasts cultured from the patient show almost no removal of thymine dimers after ultraviolet irradiation, and the defect is corrected when the patient's cells are fused with fibroblasts from a different affected child. Which molecular process is defective?
options: Nucleotide excision repair that removes bulky helix-distorting lesions as an oligonucleotide
Base excision repair that excises a single damaged base with a glycosylase
Mismatch repair that excises newly synthesized DNA containing mispaired bases
Direct reversal of ultraviolet photoproducts by a light-dependent photolyase
items.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from mutations in genes required for nucleotide excision repair, which excises bulky lesions such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers; correction by fusion with cells from a different patient reflects complementation of distinct genes in the same pathway. Base excision repair handles small non-helix-distorting lesions such as deaminated bases, mismatch repair corrects replication errors, and humans have no photolyase activity.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 2-day-old male infant becomes lethargic and tachypneic after his second feeding. Laboratory testing shows hyperammonemia, a markedly elevated plasma citrulline and heavy orotic aciduria on urine organic acid analysis. Which enzyme is deficient?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase in the mitochondrial matrix
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix
Argininosuccinate lyase in the cytosol
Arginase I in the cytosol
items.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency allows carbamoyl phosphate to accumulate and spill into the pyrimidine pathway, producing orotic aciduria with hyperammonemia and elevated citrulline because citrulline synthesis from the accumulated substrate continues. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency causes hyperammonemia with low citrulline and no orotic acid, argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes citrulline accumulation with argininosuccinate in the urine, and arginase deficiency causes hyperargininemia.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy with intellectual disability and dystonia repeatedly bites his lower lip and fingertips, and he has had several episodes of painful joint swelling. Serum uric acid and 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion are both markedly increased. A deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
options: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase
Xanthine oxidase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
items.explanation: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase salvages hypoxanthine and guanine; its deficiency diverts phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate into de novo purine synthesis, causing uric acid overproduction together with neurologic dysfunction from purine depletion in the brain. Xanthine oxidase deficiency causes xanthinuria with low uric acid, adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine stones, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes hemolysis.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 1-week-old infant develops jaundice, vomiting and poor feeding after several days of milk feeding. Examination shows hepatomegaly and bilateral cataracts, urine reducing sugars are positive and a galactose tolerance test produces a prolonged rise in blood galactose. The infant is diagnosed with classic galactosemia from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase. Accumulation of which metabolite results directly from this enzyme deficiency?
options: Galactose-1-phosphate
Galactitol
Glucose-1-phosphate
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
items.explanation: Transferase deficiency blocks conversion of galactose-1-phosphate and uridine diphosphate glucose to glucose-1-phosphate and uridine diphosphate galactose, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in liver, kidney and brain and drives the hepatic and renal injury of the disease. Galactitol accumulates in the lens through aldose reductase and explains the cataracts, but it is not the substrate of the deficient enzyme and does not account for the organ injury.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A malnourished 58-year-old man reports fatigue, leg pain and bleeding gums. Examination shows perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew-shaped hairs, splinter hemorrhages and poor healing of an old wound. Which biochemical reaction is most directly impaired?
options: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen
Sulfation of glycosaminoglycan chains using activated sulfate
Carboxylation of glutamate residues in coagulation factors
Hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the renal proximal tubule
items.explanation: Ascorbate is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, whose hydroxylysine-derived cross-links stabilize the collagen triple helix, so vitamin C deficiency causes fragile connective tissue with hemorrhage and poor wound healing. The carboxylase reaction of clotting factors requires vitamin K, sulfation uses adenosine 3-phosphate 5-phosphosulfate, and renal 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D depends on intact vitamin D metabolism rather than ascorbate.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A traveler who drank untreated stream water develops voluminous watery diarrhea without blood or mucus. Stool electrolyte analysis shows secretion of chloride and water into the intestinal lumen, and mucosal biopsy shows persistently elevated intracellular cyclic AMP in enterocytes. The causative toxin covalently modifies which signaling protein?
options: The stimulatory G protein alpha subunit by ADP-ribosylation
The inhibitory G protein alpha subunit by ADP-ribosylation
The beta-gamma subunits of the G protein by phosphorylation
Adenylyl cyclase by glycosylation of its catalytic domain
items.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit and locks it in the guanosine triphosphate bound state, keeping adenylyl cyclase active, raising cyclic AMP and driving CFTR-mediated chloride and water secretion. Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates the inhibitory alpha subunit instead, and neither toxin phosphorylates or glycosylates adenylyl cyclase.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A cell-free translation system produces a secretory protein that remains full length in the cytosol when signal recognition particle function is removed, and no protein appears inside microsomal vesicles. Which step of co-translational protein targeting depends on the signal recognition particle?
options: Arrest of translation and docking of the ribosome onto the rough endoplasmic reticulum translocon
Cleavage of the signal peptide by signal peptidase inside the endoplasmic reticulum lumen
Attachment of N-linked oligosaccharides to asparagine residues in the lumen
Folding of the completed protein assisted by calnexin in the lumen
items.explanation: The signal recognition particle binds the emerging signal peptide and the ribosome, pauses translation and delivers the complex to the signal recognition particle receptor on the rough endoplasmic reticulum so translocation can resume. Signal peptide cleavage, N-linked glycosylation and chaperone-assisted folding all occur after or independently of signal recognition particle action.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: Hepatocytes cultured in lipid-depleted medium rapidly increase transcription of HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor, and transcription falls again when cholesterol is added back to the medium. Which mechanism mediates this sterol-sensitive regulation?
options: Sterol-dependent proteolytic release of a membrane-bound transcription factor fragment
Direct binding of cholesterol to the promoter region of the reductase gene
Allosteric inhibition of RNA polymerase II by accumulating bile acids
Receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylation of the reductase protein
items.explanation: When cellular cholesterol is low, SCAP escorts SREBP from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, where site-1 and site-2 proteases release the amino terminal domain, which enters the nucleus and activates sterol response elements. Excess cholesterol retains the complex in the endoplasmic reticulum through Insig proteins, so no transcription factor fragment reaches the nucleus.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: Within seconds of epinephrine binding to a hepatocyte receptor, glycogen breakdown accelerates. Assuming glycogen phosphorylase begins in the less active b form, which covalent modification directly generates the active a form?
options: Phosphorylation of the enzyme by phosphorylase kinase
Dephosphorylation of the enzyme by protein phosphatase 1
Adenylylation of the enzyme by a heterotrimeric G protein
Polyubiquitination of the enzyme by a mitotic ligase
items.explanation: Epinephrine signaling through a stimulatory G protein raises cyclic AMP, activates protein kinase A, which activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b and converts it to the active a form. Protein phosphatase 1 removes the phosphate and inactivates the enzyme during the refeeding state.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A dividing cell is incubated with 15N-glutamine, 13C-aspartate and radiolabeled bicarbonate, and all three labels are recovered in the pyrimidine ring of newly synthesized nucleotides. Which enzyme catalyzes the first committed step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II in the cytosol
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix
Amidophosphoribosyltransferase in the cytosol
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase on the inner mitochondrial membrane
items.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II condenses bicarbonate and glutamine-derived ammonia with two molecules of ATP in the cytosol and commits nitrogen and carbon to the pyrimidine ring, after which aspartate contributes the remaining atoms. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I feeds the urea cycle, amidophosphoribosyltransferase is the first committed purine enzyme, and dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is a later pyrimidine step.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 5-day-old infant becomes irritable and feeds poorly, and a sweet odor is noted in the urine. Examination alternates between hypotonia and hypertonia with opisthotonus, and plasma amino acid analysis shows a markedly elevated leucine with normal phenylalanine and methionine. The deficient enzyme complex normally catalyzes which reaction?
options: Oxidative decarboxylation of the branched-chain alpha-keto acids
Transamination of phenylalanine with alpha-ketoglutarate
Hydroxylation of phenylalanine to form tyrosine
Hydroxymethylation of serine for one-carbon transfer
items.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which oxidatively decarboxylates the keto acids derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine, so those branched-chain amino acids accumulate and cause neurotoxicity. Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria with elevated phenylalanine rather than leucine, and the transamination and serine hydroxymethyltransferase reactions in the other options do not handle branched-chain substrates.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with tendon xanthomas has an LDL cholesterol of 300 mg/dL on a low-fat diet, and his mother suffered a myocardial infarction at age 42. Cultured fibroblasts bind normal amounts of labeled LDL at the cell surface at 4 degrees Celsius but fail to internalize it when warmed to 37 degrees, and immunostaining for the LDL receptor is normal. Which abnormality is most likely?
options: A mutation in the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor that abolishes clustering in coated pits
Complete absence of LDL receptor protein on the hepatocyte surface
Overproduction of apolipoprotein B-100 that saturates receptor-mediated uptake
Deficiency of lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase impairing cholesterol esterification
items.explanation: Receptors that reach the surface and bind ligand but cannot be endocytosed have lost the internalization signal in their short cytoplasmic tail, a phenotype also produced by adaptor protein deficiency, whereas classical familial hypercholesterolemia usually reflects absent or misfolded receptor protein. Overproduced apolipoprotein B-100 would not give normal surface binding with failed internalization, and lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency causes corneal opacities with low high-density lipoprotein.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 4-year-old with a gray pharyngeal membrane, neck swelling and low-grade fever later develops heart block. The exotoxin produced by the causative organism ADP-ribosylates a eukaryotic elongation factor and halts protein synthesis in host cells. Which factor is the target?
options: Elongation factor 2 carrying a diphthamide modification
Elongation factor 1 alpha delivering aminoacyl-tRNA
Initiation factor 2 positioning the initiator tRNA
Signal recognition particle targeting ribosomes to the endoplasmic reticulum
items.explanation: Diphtheria toxin, encoded by a beta-phage lysogenizing Corynebacterium diphtheriae, ADP-ribosylates the unique histidine-derived diphthamide residue of elongation factor 2 and freezes translocation, so translation stops in myocardial and other cells. Elongation factor 1 alpha and initiation factor 2 are not ADP-ribosylated by this toxin, and the signal recognition particle is not a translation factor subject to this modification.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Biochemistry and Molecular Biology

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops generalized edema, frothy urine and a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL with 8 g of protein in a 24-hour urine collection. Urinalysis shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts. Which change in the Starling forces across capillaries most directly drives the edema?
options: Reduced lymphatic drainage caused by interstitial fibrosis
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from severe hypoalbuminemia
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure caused by venous obstruction
Increased interstitial oncotic pressure from trapped albumin
items.explanation: Albumin is the principal determinant of plasma oncotic pressure, so heavy urinary loss lowers it and shifts net filtration outward at peripheral and splanchnic capillaries, while secondary sodium and water retention from effective volume contraction amplifies the edema. Elevated capillary hydrostatic pressure characterizes venous congestion, and interstitial oncotic pressure falls rather than rises when albumin is lost.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has an arterial pH of 7.20, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 24 mmHg and a bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L. Using Winter's formula, which interpretation of the measured partial pressure of carbon dioxide is correct?
options: It is markedly elevated, indicating primary hypoventilation
It lies within the predicted range of 24 to 28 mmHg, indicating appropriate respiratory compensation
It is lower than predicted, indicating an additional respiratory alkalosis
It is higher than predicted, indicating an additional respiratory acidosis
items.explanation: Winter's formula predicts the expected partial pressure of carbon dioxide as 1.5 times the measured bicarbonate plus 8, with a range of plus or minus 2, giving 26 plus or minus 2 or 24 to 28 mmHg here, and the measured value of 24 falls inside that range, so no second acid-base disorder is present.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A premature infant has a continuous machinery-like murmur just below the left clavicle, bounding peripheral pulses and a blood pressure of 96/40 mmHg. Which hemodynamic change accounts for the wide pulse pressure?
options: Reduced left ventricular filling that lowers systolic pressure while diastolic pressure rises
Continuous run-off of blood from the aorta into the pulmonary circulation lowering diastolic pressure
Increased stroke volume from tricuspid regurgitation raising systolic pressure only
Systemic vasoconstriction that raises both systolic and diastolic pressures together
items.explanation: A patent ductus arteriosus allows left-to-right shunting throughout the cardiac cycle, so aortic diastolic pressure falls, the pulse pressure widens and the murmur is continuous. Tricuspid regurgitation does not widen the arterial pulse pressure, systemic vasoconstriction raises diastolic pressure rather than lowering it, and reduced ventricular filling would narrow rather than widen the pulse pressure.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with exertional syncope has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to both carotids with a delayed carotid upstroke. Catheterization shows a peak left ventricular pressure of 210 mmHg with simultaneous aortic pressure of 130/80 mmHg. Which change in the left ventricular pressure-volume loop is expected?
options: An earlier aortic valve opening because afterload is reduced
An increased end-systolic volume because the ventricle must generate supranormal pressure to eject
A decreased end-diastolic volume because filling occurs at lower pressure
An increased stroke volume because ejection time is prolonged
items.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis raises afterload, so the ventricle ejects against a fixed obstruction, empties less completely and ends systole with a larger residual volume while developing concentric hypertrophy and increased wall stress. Stroke volume eventually falls, filling pressures rise later in the disease, and aortic valve opening is delayed rather than early because intraventricular pressure must build higher.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A bedridden patient suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea and hypoxemia. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.49, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mmHg, partial pressure of oxygen 58 mmHg and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. Which derangement is primarily responsible?
options: Increased oxygen affinity of hemoglobin shifting the dissociation curve left
Ventilation of alveoli that have lost perfusion, increasing physiologic dead space
Global hypoventilation with retention of carbon dioxide
Right-to-left intrapulmonary shunting through arteriovenous malformations
items.explanation: An acute pulmonary embolus removes perfusion from ventilated lung units, so ventilation goes to alveoli with no blood flow, physiologic dead space rises and the ventilation to perfusion ratio increases; the resulting mismatch produces hypoxemia with a widened gradient. Pure hypoventilation raises rather than lowers the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and shunting through malformations or a shifted curve does not explain an embolic event.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: Units of red blood cells stored for 28 days are transfused into an anemic patient. Within hours the transfused cells show markedly reduced levels of a glycolytic intermediate that normally stabilizes the deoxygenated state of hemoglobin. Which consequence follows for oxygen delivery?
options: A shortened red blood cell lifespan caused by oxidative membrane damage
A left-shifted dissociation curve with increased oxygen affinity and impaired unloading in tissues
A right-shifted dissociation curve with enhanced unloading in tissues
An increased capacity to carry carbon dioxide in venous blood
items.explanation: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate is consumed during storage and low levels shift the curve left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly and tissue unloading is transiently impaired until the cells regenerate it. A right shift, which occurs with acidosis, hypercapnia, fever and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, would enhance unloading, and carbon dioxide carriage is described by the Haldane effect rather than by this change.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with hypercalcemia and long-term lithium use passes 6 L of dilute urine daily. After infusion of hypertonic saline, plasma osmolality rises above 295 mOsm/kg and plasma ADH is high, yet urine osmolality remains below 300 mOsm/kg. Which defect explains this response?
options: Osmotic diuresis from glycosuria in the proximal tubule
End-organ resistance to ADH with failure to insert aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct
Failure of the posterior pituitary to release ADH
Excess secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide blocking water reabsorption
items.explanation: The pituitary responds appropriately but the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine, which is the definition of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and hypercalcemia and lithium produce it by disrupting V2 receptor signaling and aquaporin-2 trafficking. Central diabetes insipidus would show low ADH, atrial natriuretic peptide does not block water channels, and glucosuria produces isosthenuric rather than frankly dilute urine.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 2-year-old with three days of watery diarrhea has sunken eyes and a capillary refill of 3 seconds. Laboratory values are pH 7.25, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, sodium 138 mEq/L, chloride 118 mEq/L, potassium 3.0 mEq/L and an anion gap of 10. Which acid-base disorder results from this illness?
options: A respiratory acidosis caused by compensatory hypoventilation
A non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate
An anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by tissue hypoperfusion and lactate accumulation
A metabolic alkalosis caused by loss of gastric acid with contraction of extracellular fluid
items.explanation: Diarrhea loses bicarbonate-rich fluid directly, so the anion gap remains normal while chloride rises as the balancing anion, giving a hyperchloremic non-anion-gap acidosis. Vomiting loses hydrogen and produces a metabolic alkalosis, shock raises lactate and widens the gap, and the low carbon dioxide here is the expected respiratory compensation rather than primary respiratory acidosis.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 68-year-old with a large anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction becomes cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 84/60 mmHg, jugular venous distention, pulmonary crackles and a heart rate of 112 per minute. Which hemodynamic profile is most likely?
options: Normal cardiac output with isolated impairment of diastolic relaxation
Low cardiac index with elevated left and right-sided filling pressures
Low systemic vascular resistance with a high cardiac index and warm flushed skin
Low central venous pressure with reduced preload and a hyperdynamic ventricle
items.explanation: Loss of contractile mass after a large infarction lowers cardiac output while blood backs up, raising right atrial and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures and producing cold clammy skin, congestion and hypotension. Distributive shock shows low resistance with warm skin and a high index, hypovolemia shows low filling pressures, and isolated diastolic dysfunction would not cause frank hypotension with congestion.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 55-year-old with a ruptured appendix has a temperature of 39.4 degrees Celsius, blood pressure of 92/54 mmHg, warm flushed extremities, a cardiac index of 4.8 L/min/m2 and a systemic vascular resistance of 600 dyn s cm-5. Which mechanism most directly produces the hypotension?
options: Tamponade physiology with equalized diastolic pressures and obstructed ventricular filling
Inducible nitric oxide synthase activity causing arteriolar vasodilation and low systemic vascular resistance
Depressed myocardial contractility with a reduced stroke volume and a low cardiac index
Loss of intravascular volume from hemorrhage with reduced preload and low filling pressures
items.explanation: In early septic shock inflammatory mediators, especially nitric oxide from inducible nitric oxide synthase, dilate arterioles so blood pressure falls despite a high cardiac output, giving warm flushed skin and a low measured resistance. Cardiogenic shock lowers the index with high pressures, hemorrhage lowers filling pressures, and tamponade obstructs filling with narrow pulse pressure rather than a warm hyperdynamic picture.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: Chyme with a pH below 4.5 enters the duodenum and triggers release of a circulating hormone that acts on pancreatic duct cells, producing copious bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes the lumen. Which cell type and second messenger mediate this response?
options: Chief cells stimulated by acetylcholine with cyclic GMP as the second messenger
Ductal cells stimulated by secretin with cyclic AMP as the second messenger
Acinar cells stimulated by cholecystokinin with calcium and IP3 as second messengers
Ductal cells stimulated by gastrin with protein kinase C as the second messenger
items.explanation: Secretin from intestinal S cells raises cyclic AMP in pancreatic duct cells, driving secretion of water and bicarbonate that neutralizes gastric acid, while cholecystokinin and acetylcholine act on acinar cells to release enzyme-rich juice through calcium-dependent pathways. Gastrin acts mainly on parietal and enterochromaffin-like cells in the stomach rather than on pancreatic ducts.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and a firm nontender goiter has a thyroid-stimulating hormone of 22 mIU/mL and a free thyroxine of 0.4 ng/dL. Which mechanism explains the elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone?
options: Ectopic secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone by a hepatic tumor
Loss of negative feedback on the anterior pituitary from deficient circulating thyroid hormone
Autonomous thyroid hormone production suppressing pituitary thyrotroph output
Excess hypothalamic dopamine suppressing thyrotropin-releasing hormone release
items.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism removes the negative feedback of thyroxine and triiodothyronine on thyrotrophs, so thyrotropin-releasing hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone rise and the gland enlarges, as in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Autonomous hormone production and ectopic hormone secretion suppress thyroid-stimulating hormone rather than raise it, and dopamine restrains prolactin more than thyrotropin.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 66-year-old smoker with chronic dyspnea and decreased breath sounds has spirometry showing an FEV1 of 45 percent predicted, an FEV1 to FVC ratio of 0.55 and a total lung capacity of 130 percent predicted. Which mechanical change explains the elevated total lung capacity?
options: Restrictive chest wall deformity limiting maximal lung expansion
Premature airway closure during expiration increasing residual volume and hyperinflating the lungs
Increased elastic recoil emptying the lungs rapidly at low volumes
Weak inspiratory muscles reducing maximal inspiratory pressure and total volumes
items.explanation: Loss of alveolar attachments and small airway collapse in emphysema cause expiratory flow limitation and air trapping, so residual volume and functional residual capacity rise and total lung capacity increases. Restriction from chest wall or parenchymal disease lowers total lung capacity, and increased recoil would lower rather than raise it.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A healthy adult has fasted for 24 hours, yet plasma glucose remains near 70 mg/dL. Which set of hormonal changes most directly sustains hepatic glucose output during the fast?
options: Increased insulin with increased thyroid hormone raising glucose utilization
Suppressed insulin with increased glucagon, cortisol, growth hormone and epinephrine
Increased insulin with suppressed glucagon promoting glycogen storage
Increased amylin with suppressed cortisol slowing glucose mobilization
items.explanation: Falling insulin removes the brake on gluconeogenesis while a rising glucagon to insulin ratio plus cortisol, growth hormone and epinephrine drive glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose. The other combinations would favor glucose disposal or storage rather than sustained hepatic output.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A healthy 25-year-old runs on a treadmill to maximal exertion. Compared with rest, which combination of cardiovascular changes occurs?
options: Decreased myocardial oxygen consumption with a narrowed arteriovenous oxygen difference
Increased heart rate and stroke volume raising cardiac output with splanchnic blood flow falling
Decreased heart rate with increased stroke volume keeping cardiac output unchanged
Increased parasympathetic tone slowing the heart with reduced skeletal muscle perfusion
items.explanation: Exercise increases sympathetic activity and withdraws vagal tone, raising heart rate and stroke volume so cardiac output can rise several fold while blood is redistributed away from the splanchnic and renal beds toward skeletal muscle, and the arteriovenous oxygen difference widens as more oxygen is extracted by working muscle.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Physiology and Pathophysiology

items.stem: A 40-year-old injection drug user has a tender fluctuant abscess that drains purulent material. Culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive, and susceptibility testing shows resistance to oxacillin and to all beta-lactams except ceftaroline. Which mechanism explains this resistance pattern?
options: A plasmid-mediated macrolide esterase destroying the drug
Reduced outer membrane porin permeability in a gram-negative organism
A plasmid-borne mecA gene product with low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics
An extended-spectrum beta-lactamase hydrolyzing the beta-lactam ring
items.explanation: mecA encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a, which binds beta-lactams with very low affinity, so methicillin-resistant staphylococci resist penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems and only newer agents such as ceftaroline that bind the altered target remain active. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases occur in gram-negative bacilli, macrolide esterases affect macrolides, and porin loss is a gram-negative resistance mechanism.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 20-year-old college student presents with fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity and a petechial rash over the trunk. Lumbar puncture shows 4500 leukocytes per microliter with 90 percent neutrophils, glucose 18 mg/dL, protein 220 mg/dL and gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Which organism and virulence factor are most likely?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae with a choline-binding capsule
Listeria monocytogenes with internalin-mediated epithelial entry
Neisseria meningitidis with a sialylated polysaccharide capsule
Haemophilus influenzae type b with a polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule
items.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils together with petechiae in a young adult indicate Neisseria meningitidis, whose sialic acid-rich capsule resists complement-mediated lysis and phagocytosis and, in fulminant disease, accompanies adrenal hemorrhage. Haemophilus influenzae is a gram-negative coccus but not a diplococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus, and Listeria is a gram-positive rod.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 15-year-old who has been using a tampon for 18 hours develops fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma, vomiting and multiorgan dysfunction. Cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters. The secreted toxin binds the outer face of major histocompatibility class II and the V region of the T-cell receptor. Which mechanism produces the illness?
options: Immune complex deposition in glomerular capillaries
Antibody-mediated blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Polyclonal T-cell activation with a massive cytokine storm from superantigen crosslinking
Opsonization of the organism by IgG with consumption of complement
items.explanation: Toxic shock syndrome toxin 1 is a superantigen that crosslinks major histocompatibility class II on antigen-presenting cells with the V beta region of the T-cell receptor, activating up to a fifth of T cells at once and releasing tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1 and interleukin 2, which produce capillary leak, hypotension and multiorgan failure without requiring antigen specificity.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: An 8-year-old develops migratory polyarthritis, low-grade fever, subcutaneous nodules over the shins and a new murmur of mitral regurgitation three weeks after an untreated sore throat. Which mechanism best explains the valvular injury?
options: Deposition of IgA immune complexes in the endocardium
Superantigen-mediated destruction of myocardial cells
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein epitopes and cardiac myosin driving cross-reactive antibodies and T cells
Direct bacterial invasion of the valve forming septic vegetations
items.explanation: Acute rheumatic fever is an immune-mediated poststreptococcal disease in which antibodies and T cells cross-react with streptococcal antigens that resemble cardiac myosin and other self tissues, producing pancarditis with Aschoff bodies. No viable organism resides on the valve, which distinguishes this from infective endocarditis, and IgA complex deposition and superantigens do not explain the disease.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 35-year-old with a 3-month cough, night sweats and weight loss has bilateral upper lobe cavities and sputum containing acid-fast bacilli. Lung biopsy shows caseating granulomas packed with epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. Which immune mechanism produces this pattern?
options: IgE-mediated eosinophil degranulation around the organisms
Interleukin 4 driven alternatively activated macrophages producing fibrosis
CD4 T helper 1 lymphocytes secreting interferon gamma that activate macrophages to contain the bacilli
CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes lysing infected pneumocytes
items.explanation: Intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis persists within macrophages, and interleukin 12 driven Th1 cells release interferon gamma and tumor necrosis factor that activate macrophages to form granulomas with caseous necrosis, which contains but does not sterilize the infection. Loss of this axis through human immunodeficiency virus or tumor necrosis factor blockade allows reactivation, and the other mechanisms do not produce caseating granulomas.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 6-year-old with a painful vesicular rash on the cheek has a Tzanck preparation made from the base of a scraped vesicle that shows multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions. Which statement about this finding is correct?
options: It detects poxvirus inclusion bodies in the cytoplasm of infected keratinocytes
It is positive only after the virus has been isolated in cell culture
It confirms infection with a herpesvirus but cannot distinguish herpes simplex virus from varicella-zoster virus
It is specific for herpes simplex virus type 1 and excludes varicella-zoster virus
items.explanation: The Tzanck smear shows virus-induced cell fusion and Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions and is positive for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 as well as varicella-zoster virus, so typing requires direct fluorescent antibody testing or polymerase chain reaction. Clinical context and antigen testing distinguish the viruses, poxviruses show cytoplasmic inclusions, and the smear does not depend on prior culture.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 30-year-old with oral thrush, oral hairy leukoplakia and a CD4 count of 88 cells per microliter is found to have human immunodeficiency virus infection. A viral isolate from the patient efficiently infects activated CD4 T lymphocytes but fails to infect macrophages. Which envelope and coreceptor interaction accounts for this tropism?
options: Glycoprotein 41 binding CCR5 without CD4 engagement
The Nef protein binding the interleukin 2 receptor alpha chain
Glycoprotein 120 binding CD4 and then the CXCR4 coreceptor
Glycoprotein 120 binding CD4 and then the CCR5 coreceptor
items.explanation: T-cell tropic X4 strains use CXCR4 as the coreceptor after CD4 binding and preferentially infect T lymphocytes, whereas macrophage-tropic R5 strains use CCR5 and infect macrophages as well as T cells, with a switch to CXCR4 use often accompanying disease progression. Glycoprotein 41 mediates membrane fusion only after glycoprotein 120 engagement, and Nef downregulates CD4 and major histocompatibility class I rather than mediating entry.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A patient screened during pregnancy is negative for hepatitis B surface antigen but positive for IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen, with total antibody to hepatitis B core antigen also positive and no surface antibody detectable. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Immunity resulting from successful vaccination
Coinfection with hepatitis D requiring immunoglobulin
Recent infection during the window period when surface antigen has fallen below the level of detection
Chronic hepatitis B infection with high infectivity
items.explanation: During recovery from acute hepatitis B, surface antigen disappears before surface antibody appears, so IgM antibody to the core antigen marks the window period of recent infection. Chronic infection shows surface antigen with total core antibody and absent surface antibody, vaccination produces isolated surface antibody without core antibody, and hepatitis D requires surface antigen for its envelope.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 38-year-old with a CD4 count of 45 cells per microliter develops worsening headache, nausea and cranial nerve palsies. Cerebrospinal fluid shows an opening pressure above 300 mm of water, 60 white cells per microliter with 70 percent lymphocytes, protein of 68 mg/dL, glucose of 28 mg/dL and an encapsulated budding yeast on India ink. Which virulence factor most directly aids survival of this organism?
options: Protein A that binds the Fc region of IgG on neutrophils
A hyaluronic acid layer that prevents attachment to endothelium
A glucuronoxylomannan polysaccharide capsule that inhibits phagocytosis and complement
A mycolic acid-rich cell wall that resists oxidative burst
items.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is protected by its polysaccharide capsule, which blocks phagocytosis, depletes complement, interferes with antigen presentation and is shed into tissues and fluid, and the organism also uses urease and melanin to persist in the central nervous system. Mycolic acids belong to mycobacteria, protein A is a staphylococcal surface protein, and hyaluronic acid capsules are characteristic of group A streptococci.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A man with a CD4 count of 60 cells per microliter has had 6 weeks of watery nonbloody abdominal cramps and a 5 kg weight loss. Stool examination shows acid-fast oocysts measuring 4 to 6 micrometers, and metronidazole plus antibacterial therapy has produced no improvement. Which organism is responsible?
options: Giardia lamblia
Clostridioides difficile
Cryptosporidium parvum
Entamoeba histolytica
items.explanation: Acid-fast oocysts of Cryptosporidium in advanced human immunodeficiency virus infection cause chronic, potentially life-threatening secretory diarrhea with no reliably effective antiprotozoal therapy beyond immune reconstitution. Entamoeba histolytica invades the colonic mucosa causing bloody diarrhea with trophozoites that ingest red cells, Giardia produces fatty malabsorptive diarrhea and is not acid-fast, and Clostridioides difficile follows antibiotic exposure with toxin-mediated colitis.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: An adolescent has had two episodes of disseminated Neisseria meningitidis infection. Classical and alternative pathway assays including C3 are normal, but the terminal complement components are not detectable and patient serum fails to lyse sensitized red blood cells in a membrane attack complex assay. Which deficiency is responsible?
options: Deficiency of mannose-binding lectin
Deficiency of decay-accelerating factor
Deficiency of a terminal complement component from C5 through C9
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor
items.explanation: The membrane attack complex formed by C5b through C9 lyses gram-negative organisms, and deficiency of any terminal component predisposes to recurrent and invasive Neisseria infections because the organisms survive the complement attack. C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, mannose-binding lectin deficiency impairs early lectin pathway opsonization in childhood, and decay-accelerating factor deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A group A Rh-negative recipient of group A Rh-positive red cells five days ago now has falling hemoglobin, mild jaundice and a positive direct antiglobulin test showing IgG and C3d on her red cells, while antibody screening newly identifies anti-D. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is operating?
options: Type III hypersensitivity with circulating immune complex deposition
Type IV hypersensitivity with cytotoxic CD8 T cells attacking endothelium
Type II hypersensitivity with IgG against the D antigen fixing complement onto the red cell
Type I hypersensitivity with IgE crosslinking mast cells
items.explanation: Anti-D is an IgG antibody raised against the Rh D antigen on donor red cells, and antigen antibody complexes on the cell surface fix complement and recruit Fc receptor bearing macrophages in the spleen, which defines a type II reaction and a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction. Type I reactions require IgE, type III involves soluble complexes, and type IV requires sensitized T cells.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: After a first injection of a protein antigen, the earliest serum antibody is a pentamer with 10 binding sites that fixes complement efficiently but does not cross the placenta, and its affinity for the antigen rises in the weeks that follow. Which statement about this primary response is correct?
options: IgA is the first isotype produced and is secreted before any IgM is detectable
IgE is the first isotype and primes mast cells during the primary response
IgM predominates early with lower affinity, and T-dependent class switching later produces high-affinity IgG
IgG appears first with high affinity and no requirement for helper T cells
items.explanation: The primary response begins with pentameric IgM encoded in germline configuration with limited somatic hypermutation, then germinal center reactions generate class-switched, higher affinity IgG, IgA or IgE depending on cytokine signals, and the secondary response is faster and of higher affinity. IgG appears later in the primary response, secretory IgA follows mucosal or switched responses, and IgE is not the first isotype.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: During T-cell development in the thymus, a double-positive thymocyte whose receptor binds self-peptide presented by cortical epithelial cells with moderate affinity receives a survival signal, while a thymocyte whose receptor binds the same complex with high affinity is induced to undergo apoptosis. Which events do these observations describe?
options: V(D)J recombination followed by class switch recombination
Clonal anergy induction followed by regulatory T-cell differentiation in the periphery
Positive selection for major histocompatibility restriction followed by negative selection against strong self-reactivity
Negative selection in the bone marrow followed by clonal expansion in secondary lymphoid tissue
items.explanation: Cortical thymic epithelial cells positively select thymocytes that recognize self major histocompatibility molecules, which confers MHC restriction and fixes CD4 or CD8 lineage, and medullary epithelial cells expressing tissue antigens through the autoimmune regulator then delete strongly self-reactive clones, establishing central tolerance. The options describing recombination or peripheral anergy do not match these two selection steps.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A pregnant woman is advised to receive an inactivated influenza vaccine but to avoid live attenuated preparations, and her newborn is to receive a recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine that contains no infectious agent. Which statement comparing these vaccine types is correct?
options: Live attenuated vaccines are preferred for patients with severe combined immunodeficiency
Subunit vaccines contain attenuated organisms that have been freeze-inactivated

Inactivated and subunit vaccines cannot replicate and mainly induce helper T-cell dependent antibody, while live attenuated vaccines replicate and can induce broader immunity but are avoided in pregnancy
Inactivated vaccines replicate briefly in the host to mimic natural infection
items.explanation: Inactivated, subunit, toxoid and conjugate vaccines are non-replicating, require adjuvant and repeat dosing, and drive mainly humoral immunity, so they are safe in pregnancy and in immunodeficiency. Live attenuated vaccines such as measles mumps rubella and varicella replicate and can cause disease in immunodeficient or pregnant patients, and the description of freeze-inactivated organisms does not apply to subunit antigens.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Microbiology and Immunology

items.stem: A 55-year-old with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy is started on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor for renal protection, and three weeks later he develops a persistent dry cough that disturbs his sleep. Which mechanism best explains this adverse effect?
options: Direct irritant effect of a sulfhydryl group on the tracheal mucosa
Antagonism of angiotensin II at type 1 receptors in airway smooth muscle
Inhibition of cyclooxygenase in the bronchial epithelium
Decreased degradation of bradykinin and substance P in the pulmonary circulation
items.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is also kininase II, so inhibiting it raises bradykinin and substance P in the lung, which irritates airway sensory nerves and causes a dry cough in about one in ten patients, and angiotensin receptor blockers avoid this by leaving bradykinin breakdown intact. Sulfhydryl groups were once blamed but cough occurs with agents that lack them, and cyclooxygenase inhibition is the action of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 40-year-old with type 1 diabetes starts propranolol for tremor and migraine prophylaxis. During a hypoglycemic episode with a glucose of 42 mg/dL he reports no palpitations and no tremor, though his skin is wet with sweat. Which adverse effect of nonselective beta blockade is illustrated?
options: Enhanced insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells worsening the hypoglycemia
Increased hepatic glycogenolysis causing rebound hyperglycemia
Blockade of presynaptic alpha 2 receptors increasing norepinephrine release
Masking of adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia while cholinergic sweating persists
items.explanation: Beta-2 mediated tachycardia, tremor and anxiety are the adrenergic alarms of hypoglycemia, and nonselective beta blockade blunts them while sympathetic cholinergic sweating remains intact, so patients may fail to recognize hypoglycemia. Insulin secretion is not enhanced by beta blockade, hepatic glycogenolysis is reduced rather than increased by beta-2 block, and the presynaptic alpha 2 mechanism does not explain this pattern.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: Penicillin G is started for streptococcal endocarditis. The drug mimics the terminal dipeptide of the peptidoglycan precursor and covalently acylates the active site serine of a membrane-anchored enzyme, preventing crosslinking of glycan strands until the cell lyses. Which target is acylated?
options: The enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase of mycolic acid synthesis
The A subunit of DNA gyrase in the cytosol
The 16S ribosomal RNA of the 30S subunit
The transpeptidase domain of a penicillin-binding protein
items.explanation: Beta-lactams are structural analogs of D-alanyl-D-alanine and acylate the transpeptidase active site of penicillin-binding proteins, blocking crosslinking of peptidoglycan so autolysins lyse the growing cell. Isoniazid targets the mycolic acid pathway, fluoroquinolones target DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, and aminoglycosides bind the 30S ribosomal subunit.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A patient with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium bacteremia is treated with linezolid after susceptibility testing. Analysis of the purified peptidoglycan precursor from the isolate shows that the terminal residue of the lipid II stem peptide is D-lactate rather than D-alanine. Which mechanism explains the resistance?
options: An altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for all beta-lactams
Efflux of the drug by an ATP-binding cassette pump specific to macrolides
Reduced outer membrane permeability with loss of a porin channel
Replacement of the terminal D-alanine with D-lactate reduces vancomycin binding affinity roughly one thousandfold
items.explanation: The vanA and vanB gene clusters direct synthesis of a modified precursor ending in D-lactate, which removes a critical hydrogen bond and drops vancomycin affinity about one thousandfold while the organism continues building cell wall. Methicillin resistance reflects mecA encoded penicillin-binding protein 2a, macrolide efflux is unrelated, and porin loss is a gram-negative mechanism.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 65-year-old takes aspirin daily after a myocardial infarction. Laboratory testing shows a bleeding time of 12 minutes with a normal prothrombin time and a normal partial thromboplastin time. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
options: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase reducing factors II, VII, IX and X
Enhanced antithrombin III inactivation of thrombin by heparan sulfate
Chelation of calcium ions preventing the contact activation pathway
Irreversible acetylation of cyclooxygenase 1 in anucleate platelets blocking thromboxane synthesis for the platelet lifespan
items.explanation: Platelets cannot synthesize new enzyme, so acetylation of cyclooxygenase 1 for the 7 to 10 day platelet lifespan abolishes thromboxane A2 and impairs aggregation, prolonging the bleeding time while plasma coagulation times remain normal. Warfarin prolongs the prothrombin time through vitamin K-dependent factors, heparin prolongs the partial thromboplastin time, and calcium chelation describes citrate or EDTA tubes.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 70-year-old started on warfarin for atrial fibrillation develops painful erythematous patches that progress to dusky purple skin lesions on the thighs and buttocks within the first 72 hours, and testing shows protein C activity at 28 percent of normal. What is the mechanism of these lesions?
options: Direct activation of factor V causing widespread microthrombi
Antibody-mediated platelet destruction causing thrombocytopenic purpura
Inhibition of plasminogen activation producing isolated failure of fibrinolysis
Rapid depletion of short-lived protein C before the procoagulant factors fall, creating transient hypercoagulability
items.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase and prevents gamma carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X as well as the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S; protein C has the shortest half-life at about 8 hours, so early dosing tips the balance toward thrombosis and causes warfarin-induced skin necrosis, which is why protein C deficiency is heparin bridged. The other mechanisms do not describe vitamin K antagonism.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A patient taking a nonselective monoamine oxidase inhibitor develops sudden severe hypertension, pounding headache, sweating and a heart rate of 104 after a meal of aged cheese and cured sausage. Which mechanism best explains this crisis?
options: Histamine blocking H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells causing acid hypersecretion
Glutamate activating NMDA receptors in the hypothalamus
Direct agonism of the drug at vascular alpha 2 receptors
Tyramine escaping intestinal metabolism displaces norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve endings
items.explanation: Monoamine oxidase in the gut normally deaminates tyramine from aged and fermented foods; inhibition allows tyramine to enter the circulation, enter sympathetic terminals through the norepinephrine transporter and displace stored norepinephrine, producing a hypertensive crisis. Management removes the offending food and uses alpha blockade such as phentolamine or nitroprusside while sympathomimetics are avoided.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A dentist notes slower onset and weaker block when lidocaine is infiltrated into an inflamed acidic abscess, and buffers the solution with bicarbonate to speed onset. Which statement best explains the reduced efficacy in infected tissue?
options: Higher extracellular pH protonates the drug so it cannot bind the channel from inside the membrane
Infection increases alpha-1-acid glycoprotein binding that removes free drug from the tissue
Inflammatory prostaglandins already occupy the sodium channel pore
Lower extracellular pH shifts the weak base toward its ionized form, reducing passage across the neuronal membrane
items.explanation: Local anesthetics cross the membrane in the uncharged form and bind the sodium channel in the ionized form from the intracellular side, so acidic tissue protonates more of the drug and less reaches the interior of the neuron. Buffering raises the pH and increases the uncharged fraction for faster onset, alpha-1-acid glycoprotein binding concerns plasma drug levels rather than tissue pH, and prostaglandins do not occlude the channel.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 25-year-old with 4 months of depressed mood tells her clinician that she is worthless, that her future holds only failure and that the world is hostile and unchanging. Her therapist has her log automatic thoughts and test them with behavioral experiments. Which model and intervention are being used?
options: Psychodynamic model with free association and interpretation
Classical conditioning model with systematic desensitization
Operant conditioning model with contingency management
Beck's cognitive model with cognitive behavioral therapy
items.explanation: Beck proposed that depression is maintained by a negative cognitive triad about the self, the world and the future together with information-processing biases, and cognitive behavioral therapy identifies and revises those thoughts with structured techniques. Systematic desensitization is a classical conditioning treatment for phobias, contingency management is operant and used in substance use disorders, and free association belongs to psychodynamic therapy.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A new screening test for a disease with a prevalence of 1 in 1000 is applied to 100000 people, and it has a sensitivity of 99 percent and a specificity of 99 percent. How many people test positive, and what proportion of those positives actually have the disease?
options: 1098 positive results of which 999 are true cases, a positive predictive value of about 91 percent
99 positive results of which all are true cases, a positive predictive value of 100 percent
1000 positive results of which 100 are true cases, a positive predictive value of 10 percent
1098 positive results of which 99 are true cases, a positive predictive value of about 9 percent
items.explanation: There are 100 cases, of whom 99 test positive, and 99900 non-cases, of whom 999 test false positive, giving 1098 positive results and a positive predictive value of 99 divided by 1098 or about 9 percent. At very low prevalence even an excellent test yields many false positives, and raising prevalence or pretest probability raises the positive predictive value.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 68-year-old with mild cognitive impairment due to early Alzheimer disease is admitted for a blood transfusion and refuses it, explaining that he does not believe he is anemic and does not want foreign blood. His daughter asks the team to transfuse him over his objection. Which principle most directly supports honoring his refusal?
options: Beneficence, which permits overriding a stated refusal when the treatment is beneficial
Nonmaleficence, because refusing an indicated transfusion causes harm
Distributive justice, because the blood supply is limited
Autonomy, supported by an assessment showing he understands, appreciates and can reason about this specific decision
items.explanation: Decision-making capacity is specific to the decision and requires understanding, appreciation, reasoning and an expression of choice; a patient who retains capacity may refuse beneficial treatment and clinicians may not substitute their judgment. Surrogate decision-making with substituted judgment or best interests applies only once capacity is lost, and nonmaleficence and justice do not authorize overriding a capacitated refusal.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: Investigators enroll 200 patients with lung cancer and 400 without the disease, then interview both groups and reconstruct occupational exposure to asbestos in the decades before diagnosis. Which study design and advantage best describe this investigation?
options: A prospective cohort study, which measures incidence directly
A randomized controlled trial, which controls confounding through random allocation
A cross-sectional survey, which provides disease incidence rates
A case-control study, efficient for rare outcomes and able to examine multiple exposures at once
items.explanation: Sampling by outcome status defines a case-control study, which is efficient for rare diseases with long latency and can evaluate many exposures, but it yields an odds ratio rather than incidence and is vulnerable to recall and selection bias. Incidence requires a cohort or a trial, randomization is absent here, and cross-sectional data give prevalence rather than incidence.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 7-year-old works hard to collect trading cards, compares his reading speed with classmates and becomes discouraged after mistakes in front of others. According to Erikson, which psychosocial conflict is at issue, and what is the outcome of unsuccessful resolution?
options: Initiative versus guilt, with unresolved conflict leading to excessive caution and fear of trying
Identity versus role confusion, with unresolved conflict leading to diffusion of values
Trust versus mistrust, with unresolved conflict leading to anxiety about feeding and care
Industry versus inferiority, with unresolved conflict leading to feelings of inadequacy and passivity
items.explanation: Erikson places industry versus inferiority in the school years from about 6 to 12 years, when children master skills and measure themselves against peers, and failure produces a sense of inadequacy. Initiative versus guilt occurs at 3 to 6 years, identity versus role confusion in adolescence, and trust versus mistrust in infancy.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A man whose partner died in the hospital the previous night shouts at a clerk over a delayed form during registration and later berates his children for a minor mess at dinner. Which defense mechanism is demonstrated?
options: Projection, attributing his own unacceptable anger to others
Reaction formation, expressing the opposite of an unacceptable impulse
Rationalization, constructing an acceptable explanation for a failure
Displacement, redirecting affect from a threatening target to a safer substitute
items.explanation: Displacement channels emotions onto a less threatening substitute when the original target is dangerous or unacceptable, which fits his anger toward staff and family after a loss. Projection would be his belief that others are angry with him, reaction formation would be exaggerated kindness masking anger, and rationalization would be a plausible but superficial justification for his behavior.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science

items.stem: A 32-year-old with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium develops polyuria, polydipsia and a serum lithium level of 1.8 mEq/L two weeks after starting indomethacin for back pain. Urine osmolality is 180 mOsm/kg with normal plasma osmolality. Which renal mechanism best explains the concentrating defect?
options: Lithium blocks the sodium-chloride cotransporter causing salt wasting in the thick ascending limb
Lithium precipitates in the proximal tubule causing acute tubular necrosis
Lithium competitively antagonizes aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor
Lithium entry through epithelial sodium channels impairs V2 receptor signaling and aquaporin-2 insertion in principal cells
items.explanation: Lithium is reabsorbed with sodium through epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct, enters principal cells and inhibits adenylyl cyclase downstream of the V2 receptor, so aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results; indomethacin lowers renal prostaglandins, reduces free water clearance and raises lithium levels further. Thiazides block the sodium chloride cotransporter, and proximal injury and mineralocorticoid blockade do not explain this pattern.
items.reference: USMLE Step 1 Content Outline - Pharmacology and Behavioral Science
